name: Network Coverage
description: The government of Berland decided to improve network coverage in his country. Berland has a unique structure: the capital in the center and $$$n$$$ cities in a circle around the capital. The capital already has a good network coverage (so the government ignores it), but the $$$i$$$-th city contains $$$a_i$$$ households that require a connection. The government designed a plan to build $$$n$$$ network stations between all pairs of neighboring cities which will maintain connections only for these cities. In other words, the $$$i$$$-th network station will provide service only for the $$$i$$$-th and the $$$(i + 1)$$$-th city (the $$$n$$$-th station is connected to the $$$n$$$-th and the $$$1$$$-st city). All network stations have capacities: the $$$i$$$-th station can provide the connection to at most $$$b_i$$$ households. Now the government asks you to check can the designed stations meet the needs of all cities or not — that is, is it possible to assign each household a network station so that each network station $$$i$$$ provides the connection to at most $$$b_i$$$ households.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains the single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 10^6$$$) — the number of cities and stations. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers ($$$1 \le a_i \le 10^9$$$) — the number of households in the $$$i$$$-th city. The third line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers ($$$1 \le b_i \le 10^9$$$) — the capacities of the designed stations. It's guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over test cases doesn't exceed $$$10^6$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print YES , if the designed stations can meet the needs of all cities, or NO otherwise (case insensitive).
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1373F — Network Coverage [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
